description: Using NOAA Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) records and NASA POWER satellite observations (2025–2026), this project investigates how the strong 2026 El Niño (+2.5°C peak) drove extreme heat across Nigeria. Comparing daily temperature and rainfall in Kano, Osogbo, and Lagos reveals a clear coastal-to-inland warming gradient (+0.24°C in Lagos, +0.42°C in Osogbo, and +1.26°C in arid Kano), demonstrating an accessible framework for early heat-stress monitoring.
summary: We developed a data-driven climate trend analysis and visualization framework tracking the 2026 El Niño event and its regional thermal and precipitation impacts across Nigeria. Addressing the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge, we analyzed multi-year Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) records from NOAA (2024–2026) alongside daily temperature and precipitation datasets from the NASA POWER Data Access Viewer for three geographically distinct Nigerian cities: Kano (North), Osogbo (South-West), and Lagos (Coast). Our analysis confirms that as the 2026 El Niño surged to +2.5°C, average temperatures across Nigeria rose along a clear coastal-to-inland gradient (+0.24°C in Lagos, +0.42°C in Osogbo, and +1.26°C in arid Kano). This work is important because it demonstrates how open-access NASA Earth observation data can power low-cost, local early heat-stress monitoring to protect vulnerable communities.
details:
What It Does & How It Works
Our project acts as a climate-trend investigation connecting global ocean warming anomalies to local weather shifts across Nigeria. Using a two-stage comparative methodology, we first tracked 3-month rolling Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) records from NOAA (2024–2026) to pinpoint when Pacific Ocean warming crossed the +0.5°C El Niño threshold and surged to its +2.5°C peak in late 2026. Second, we extracted daily satellite-derived 2-meter air temperature (T2M) and corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR) datasets from the NASA POWER Data Access Viewer (2025–2026) for three geographically distinct Nigerian cities—Kano (North), Osogbo (South-West), and Lagos (Coast). By cleaning missing-value placeholders (-999) and computing multi-year conditional averages, we identified a clear coastal-to-inland warming gradient (+0.24°C in Lagos, +0.42°C in Osogbo, and +1.26°C in arid Kano).

Tools & Software Used

  • Data Sources: NASA POWER Data Access Viewer (Version 2.0.0) and NOAA Climate Prediction Center (ONI v5/v6).
  • Analysis & Visualization: Microsoft Excel (for CSV cleaning, AVERAGEIFS conditional statistical modeling, multi-series line charts, and clustered column comparisons).
  • Documentation & Formatting: Microsoft Word / PDF with APA 7th edition academic standards.

Creativity & Factors Considered
Rather than treating Nigeria as a single uniform climate zone, we creatively selected three contrasting geographic locations—coastal (Lagos), inland tropical forest/savanna transition (Osogbo), and semi-arid Sahelian (Kano)—to test how proximity to the Atlantic Ocean moderates El Niño heat stress. We also accounted for seasonal completeness by comparing aligned January–November observation windows and filtering out unprocessed satellite fill values (-999) to ensure statistical accuracy.

Benefits & Intended Impact
This framework demonstrates that high-impact climate trend detection does not require expensive ground weather stations or complex supercomputing. By pairing free NASA Earth observation data with accessible spreadsheet analytics, local researchers, universities, and public health agencies in Nigeria can monitor emerging heatwaves early, prioritize vulnerable inland regions like Kano, and issue timely community heat-stress advisories.
